title: Beware the Sirens
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman warns policymakers against the appealing but misleading call to reduce school suspensions and permanent exclusions from above. Starting from recent statements by a Bedfordshire police commissioner and London's mayor, he argues that claims linking exclusion to later violence confuse correlation with causation, since the same pupils who are violent at school are likely to be violent afterward. He points to Scotland's restorative-approach policy and his own earlier warning to New South Wales as cases where restricting principals' powers went badly. His alternative is to reduce the need for sanctions from below through routines, structures and a behaviour curriculum, and he cites his own experience of a chaotic school with high suspensions alongside Michaela's low rates under a warm-strict policy. He closes by reframing inclusion: a policy that looks kind to the excluded pupil can be unkind to the classmates whose safety and education are put at risk.
points: Ashman argues that the statistic linking permanent exclusion to later violence reflects which pupils get excluded, not an effect of exclusion itself.
He cites Scotland, and New South Wales before its reversal, as places where limiting principals' power to suspend led to worse outcomes.
The school with the worst behaviour he worked in also had the highest suspension rate, because it had no common routines or detention system.
Inclusion policies should be judged by their effect on the other students too, including their safety and right to learn.
quotes: In Ancient Greek mythology, the sirens were creatures with a song so beautiful they lured sailors to their doom. In education, we have our own sirens luring policymakers onto the rocks.

I have no reason to doubt that the evidence shows this, but the implication that exclusion causes young people to be involved in violence is deeply misleading. It seems more likely that children who engage in violence at school, and are therefore more likely to be permanently excluded, will also engage in violence at a later point in time.
Rather than bearing down on it from above by frustrating the ability of principals to suspend, they should look to solve it from below by reducing the levels of poor behaviour. Routines. Structures.

The problem was that there was nothing else. No common routines. No detention system. If a teacher wanted to place a student in detention, they had to organise this themselves and the chances that the student would simply walk out were high.
Why do policymakers fall for calls to restrict suspensions and permanent exclusions? Inclusion sounds virtuous. Exclusion sounds mean. Who wouldn't be in favour of inclusion over exclusion?

But this is a failure of perspective. It only works if we focus exclusively on those students who are suspended or expelled. We also need to consider the other students in the school, their safety and their right to an education.
The activist retort to this is that I am using extreme examples. Sadly, these situations are not as uncommon as I would wish them to be. And schools need the tools to deal with them.
